Statins lower LDL cholesterol by reducing the liver’s production of cholesterol and increasing the liver’s ability to reabsorb cholesterol that’s already in your bloodstream. Do statins clear the arteries of plaque? Yes. Statins can reduce the amount of fatty deposits in your arteries. They can also stabilize existing plaque deposits, making them less likely to break off and cause a blood clot. Do statins lower cholesterol immediately? passages.text: Key takeaways - Statins help lower cholesterol by reducing the liver’s cholesterol production and increasing its ability to reabsorb existing cholesterol in the bloodstream. - Following your doctor’s orders, getting regular testing, and living a healthy lifestyle are essential for managing cholesterol levels while taking statins. - While statins can have side effects, they can also reduce fatty deposits in arteries and lower cholesterol levels within weeks. Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance. It’s found in every cell of the body. Your body is capable of making all the cholesterol it needs to function properly. However, the foods you eat may supplement cholesterol levels. There are two types of cholesterol: high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL). HDL is referred to as the “good” cholesterol. It helps remove excess cholesterol from your body. LDL is referred to as the “bad” cholesterol because it creates buildup in your arteries. This can lead to blocked arteries and the potential for a heart attack or stroke. This article explains how statins help lower cholesterol. It also provides tips for taking statins and managing your cholesterol levels. Doctors recommend statin medications for people with high cholesterol or people at risk of cardiovascular disease. Statins work in two ways to reduce your cholesterol: - Statins stop the production of cholesterol: Statins block an enzyme involved in making cholesterol particles. Reducing production lowers the total amount of cholesterol available in your bloodstream. - Statins help reabsorb existing cholesterol: Your body needs cholesterol to perform certain tasks. These tasks include: - helping you digest food - making hormones - absorbing vitamin D Since statins lower the amount of cholesterol your liver makes, your liver must get cholesterol from circulating blood. With statins, your liver puts LDL receptors on its surface that capture circulating LDL particles, lowering your blood cholesterol levels to prevent cholesterol from depositing in your arteries. An enzyme called hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) signals the liver that it should make more cholesterol. Statins, also called HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, block or reduce the activity of the HMG-CoA enzyme, meaning that the liver makes less LDL cholesterol. As the liver makes less LDL cholesterol, it also takes more LDL cholesterol from the blood, reducing the levels that move around the body. Statins can also help reduce triglycerides (blood fats) and may boost levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. Doctors will not prescribe statins for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding. They may not recommend statins for groups with a higher risk of side effects, including people who are over 70 years old or have liver disease, hypothyroidism, or a family history of rhabdomyolysis. They may also avoid prescribing statins to people who take drugs that have a risk of interactions. It is important for people to let a doctor know about any other medications they are taking before they begin taking statins. Statins can help lower high cholesterol levels. They cause the liver to make less low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, which reduces blood cholesterol levels and can help lower a person’s risk of heart disease and stroke. Policy Statins are prescription medications that people take to bring their cholesterol down to normal levels. Statins decrease the “bad” cholesterol that builds up in your arteries: LDL (low-density lipoprotein). High levels of LDL in your bloodstream lead to a buildup of plaque in blood vessels. This can clog your blood vessels and make it harder for blood to flow. A heart attack or stroke occurs when plaque completely clogs an artery. Statins also decrease your triglycerides and help your liver get rid of more cholesterol. They may increase your HDL (high-density lipoprotein or “good”) cholesterol. passages.text: Statins are drugs that can lower your cholesterol. They work by blocking a substance that your body needs to make cholesterol. Lowering cholesterol isn't the only benefit of taking a statin. These medicines also have been linked to a lower risk of heart disease and stroke. Statins also may help reduce the risk of certain blood clots. A number of statins are available for use in the United States. They include: - Atorvastatin (Lipitor). - Fluvastin (Lescol XL). - Lovastatin (Altoprev). - Pitavastatin (Livalo). - Pravastatin. - Rosuvastatin (Crestor). - Simvastatin (Zocor). Sometimes, a statin is combined with another heart medicine. Examples are atorvastatin-amlodipine (Caduet) and ezetimibe-simvastatin (Vytorin). Should you be on a statin? Whether you need to be on a statin depends on your cholesterol levels and other risk factors for heart and blood vessel disease. Your healthcare professional will consider all of your risk factors for heart attacks and strokes before prescribing a statin. Knowing your cholesterol numbers is a good place to start. - Total cholesterol. Most people should try to keep their total cholesterol below 200 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL), or 5.2 millimoles per liter (mmol/L). - Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. If you’ve received a diagnosis of high cholesterol and are taking statins or plan to take statins in the near future, here are some helpful tips for managing your medications and your health. Follow your doctor’s orders Your cholesterol levels are closely related to your overall health. That’s why it’s so important to adhere to your doctor’s prescription and keep your cholesterol numbers in a heart-healthy range. Don’t skip doses When it comes to drugs, skipping doses or stopping your medication without first talking with your doctor could cost you your life. A 2019 research study notes that stopping statin use was associated with a significantly increased risk of heart failure and other cardiovascular events. Get regular testing If you’re taking statins, your doctor needs to monitor your blood and overall health for signs of complications related to the medication. Make and keep regular appointments for blood tests and checkups. Often, blood tests are the first and best way for your doctor to spot a potential problem before symptoms or complications appear. If your cholesterol — particularly the LDL ("bad") type — stays high after you make healthy lifestyle changes, statins might be an option for you. Consider statins a lifelong commitment You may think that if your cholesterol goes down, you don't need a statin anymore. But if the medicine helped lower your cholesterol, you'll likely need to stay on it long term to keep your cholesterol down. If you make significant changes to your diet or lose a lot of weight, talk to your healthcare professional about whether it might be possible to control your cholesterol without medicine.
